elements.element: Customer owns Deliverables and work product created for Customer.
elements.evidence: Revised 14.2: "Customer exclusively owns every Deliverable and work product created for Customer" — the prior Vendor-ownership sentence is gone.

elements.element: Vendor assigns the Deliverables and work product to Customer.
elements.evidence: Revised 14.2: "Vendor hereby assigns to Customer all right, title, and interest in each Deliverable and work product" — present-tense assignment, correct party direction.

elements.element: Vendor retains its pre-existing intellectual property.
elements.evidence: 14.3 retained unchanged: "Vendor retains Vendor Technology," defined in 1.8 as Vendor's pre-existing software, tools, models, templates and technology.

elements.element: Customer's licence to Vendor IP embedded in Deliverables is perpetual.
elements.evidence: 13.2 (unchanged): for Vendor Technology "embedded in a Deliverable, Vendor grants Customer and its Affiliates a perpetual ... licence"; 14.3 expressly cross-refers to that perpetual licence.

elements.element: Customer's licence to embedded Vendor IP is irrevocable.
elements.evidence: 13.2: "perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free, fully paid licence."

elements.element: Customer's licence to embedded Vendor IP is royalty-free.
elements.evidence: 13.2: "royalty-free, fully paid licence to use, execute, reproduce, display, perform, modify, create derivative works from ... for Customer's business."

elements.element: Customer retains all rights in Customer Data.
elements.evidence: 14.1 (unchanged): "As between the Parties, Customer owns all Customer Data, Customer Confidential Information, Customer-provided material, and intellectual property Customer owned or developed independently of the Services." No assignment of Customer Data to Vendor appears anywhere in the rendered text.

elements.element: Any Vendor licence in Customer Data is limited to processing it solely to provide the Services.
elements.evidence: 14.1: "No right transfers to Vendor except the limited right to process that material solely to provide, secure, support, and improve the Services for Customer," reinforced by 15.1 (documented instructions only; no sale, advertising, cross-customer combination, or model training without consent). The 'secure, support, improve' verbs are all tethered to the Services 'for Customer' and confer no distribution or independent-exploitation right.

elements.element: The parties do not jointly own intellectual property.
elements.evidence: 14.4 (unchanged): "No jointly owned intellectual property is created unless the Parties sign a separate instrument identifying it and their exploitation rights" — any joint ownership requires a future signed instrument that itself fixes exploitation rights.

elements.element: Vendor may retain ownership of generic tools and know-how.
elements.evidence: 14.3 "Vendor retains Vendor Technology"; Deliverable definition 1.4 excludes "generally applicable ideas, methods, skills, and know-how retained in the unaided memory of Vendor personnel."

elements.element: Customer's licence to Deliverables is perpetual.
elements.evidence: Satisfied a fortiori: revised 14.2 vests outright ownership of every Deliverable in Customer, and the former revocable, term-limited licence is deleted, so Customer's rights are not time-bounded.

elements.element: Customer's licence to Deliverables is irrevocable.
elements.evidence: Ownership under revised 14.2 plus deletion of the words "revocable, non-transferable licence" leaves no revocation mechanic over Deliverables.

elements.element: Customer's licence to Deliverables is worldwide.
elements.evidence: Ownership under revised 14.2 carries no territorial limit; no retained sentence restricts geography of Deliverable use.

elements.element: Customer's licence to Deliverables is royalty-free.
elements.evidence: Revised 14.2 assigns all right, title and interest without any continuing royalty or fee condition; 13.2 embedded Vendor Technology is separately "royalty-free, fully paid."

elements.element: Customer may use and modify Deliverables for its business.
elements.evidence: As owner under revised 14.2 Customer may use and modify; 13.2 additionally permits modification and derivative works of any embedded Vendor Technology needed to do so.

elements.element: Customer may sublicense Deliverables for its business.
elements.evidence: The prior "non-transferable" restriction is deleted and Customer owns the Deliverables outright, so sublicensing is unimpeded; 13.2 covers Affiliates and contractor support for embedded Vendor Technology.

elements.element: Any Vendor licence in Customer Data is limited to processing it solely to provide the Services.
elements.evidence: Same operative text as at the preferred level: 14.1 "limited right to process that material solely to provide, secure, support, and improve the Services for Customer," bounded by 15.1's documented-instruction and no-sale/no-training limits.

elements.element: Customer owns Deliverables and work product created for Customer.
elements.evidence: Not a fallback element, but noted: ownership under revised 14.2 exceeds the fallback licence construct and does not conflict with any fallback item.

reasons: The edit is confined to Section 14.2: the Vendor-ownership sentence and the dependent revocable, non-transferable, term-limited licence are replaced by Customer ownership plus a present-tense Vendor assignment. Deleting the licence sentence is necessary, not cosmetic, because it is inconsistent with Customer ownership of the same subject matter.
No extras were added — no survival tail, no expense allocation, no procedure, no escrow or delivery obligation, and no duplicated licence grant alongside the ownership vesting.

Favourable existing language is retained intact: 14.1 (Customer Data ownership and limited processing right), 14.3 (Vendor Technology retention, pre-delivery identification, third-party material approval), 14.4 (no joint IP; feedback carve-outs), 13.2 (perpetual, irrevocable, worldwide, royalty-free embedded licence) and 15.1 (processing restrictions) are unchanged.

Cross-references survive: 14.3's pointer to "the perpetual licence in Section 13.2" still resolves, and 13.2's reference to Vendor Technology "embedded in a Deliverable" remains coherent now that Customer owns the Deliverable while Vendor keeps the embedded technology. No undefined term or dangling reference is created.

One drafting note, not a defect requiring repair: 14.1's processing right reads "solely to provide, secure, support, and improve the Services for Customer." The 'improve' verb is slightly wider than the checklist's 'solely to provide the Services', but it is expressly tethered to the Services for Customer and is fenced by 15.1's bar on sale, advertising, cross-customer combination and model training, so no distribution or independent-exploitation right exists and the element holds.

Both checklists are complete on the rendered text; the finding is correctly a deviation cured at the preferred level, and the margin comment accurately describes the change without promising anything absent from the operative language.
